Speech Act Theory by J.L Austin and John Searle
Why does this matter for IT professionals?
Every email, meeting, and presentation is a speech act
Understanding intent helps you communicate more effectively with colleagues and clients
Speech acts are the speaker’s utterances that convey meaning and make listeners do specific things (Austin, 1962).
According to Austin (1962), when saying a performative utterance, a speaker is simultaneously doing something.
📖 Key Insight: When we speak, we simultaneously DO something. Every utterance has a purpose.

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
Performative Utterance
That is why communication is important (verbal or non-verbal (e.g., writing and gestures) because it is the way people express what they need, want, and need to get things done
Language is central to everything – it makes us uniquely human
Utterances that are used to perform: requests, warnings, invitations, promises, predictions etcs.
Example:
“I am hungry.” expresses hunger, request for something to eat

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
Speech Act in Everyday Utterances
"You're fired!“
Expresses both the employment status of the individual in question, as well as the action by which said person's employment is ended.
"We ask that you extinguish your cigarettes at this time, and bring your tray tables and seatbacks to an upright position."
Describes the requirements of the current location, such as an airplane, while also issuing the command to stop smoking and to sit up straight.
"Would it be too much trouble for me to ask you to hand me that wrench?" functions t
Simultaneously ask two questions. The first is to ask the listener if they are capable of passing the wrench, while the second is an actual request.

Common Ground — Herbert H. Clark (1996)
Goal of communication: achieving mutual understanding between speaker and listener
What is Grounding?
Ensuring both speaker and listener reach shared understanding of what was said and meant.
Listener Must...
Notice · Hear · Understand what was said · Understand what was MEANT
Common Ground Accumulates
Shared history, cultural context, and interaction history all contribute to common ground over time.
Why Real Conversation is Messy
Incomplete sentences, pauses, overlapping turns, unintelligible utterances — all normal!
For IT Professionals
Building common ground with clients and teams reduces misunderstandings and project failures.

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
What is Professional Communication?
Communications that occur with your colleagues within an organization, professional society or organization and colleagues external to your organization
Communication is defined as a:
Two-way process of reaching mutual understanding, in which participants not only exchange (encode- decode) information, news, ideas and feelings but also create and share meaning.
In general, communication is a means of connecting people or places.
It can be categorized into verbal and non-verbal (includes gestures and writing)

Intrapersonal vs Interpersonal Skills for IT Professionals
Intrapersonal Skill
Communication with oneself
Self-talk, reflection, internal motivation and self-regulation
Self-discipline · Self-awareness · Open-mindedness · Patience
Interpersonal Skill
Communication with others
Verbal and non-verbal exchanges with colleagues, clients and teams
Assertiveness · Active Listening · Questioning · Feedback
Why It Matters
For your IT career
Strong communication skills lead to better team outcomes and client relationships
Builds trust · Reduces conflict · Increases productivity
In Action
Real examples
Team standup meeting · Client requirements gathering · Code review feedback
All require BOTH intra and interpersonal skills
💡 Knowing your own strengths and limits (intrapersonal) helps you communicate your ideas with confidence (interpersonal)

⚡ Questioning Technique
Asking questions is the key to understanding situations around us
Being curious and inquisitive is to be encouraged by questioning
Famously, Albert Einstein stated that. ‘The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existing.’

⚡ Other questioning techniques
Objective criteria
Questions that focus on the objective facts, to defuse any contentious situations
Hypothetical
When we already know the answer but are testing the responder’s– ‘what if’ questions allow exploring options without binding the parties involved
Testing
Knowledge or skills. Softening up – these questions allow us to ‘soften up’ our audience by building rapport or flattering. Often we will already know the answer to these questions
Reflective
A reflective question reflects the other person’s feelings to them, giving them feedback that these feelings are acknowledged

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2

⚡ Feedback Techniques
It gives the recipient advice, support, or constructive criticism. It includes both positive and negative aspects.
For feedback to be constructive, it ought to be:
Fair - Accurate - Specific - Formally structured - Solution - oriented - Focused on behavior, not personality

Effective Professional Writing
5-Step Approach to Professional Written Communication
Identify the objectives (am I writing to apply a job, send a proposal, seek new ideas?)
Conduct research (if it an internship job, what skills are they looking for?)
Create background (e.g., who am I, how did I come about the information? Why should they bother to read this?)
Compose a message
Follow-up

How to compose message

Clarify what the document/purpose of writing is all about
Detail the information in a clear, concise and conclusive manner
Make initiatives for the readers
End the message “nicely”

Stage 2 : Development and Writing
1. Type of presentation:
Informational
Motivational
Situational
All of the above
2. Outline the presentation, including key points for the introduction, key messages, and sequence of ideas.
3. Determine what information is needed to support your message?

Tips: Your presentation should have a clear structure, and do not forget to link them together. In such a brief allotted time, you won’t have time to do much besides summarising the main points and providing key messages you want to impart to the audience.

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
Stage 2 : Development and Writing
4. Develop the introduction, discussion, and conclusion.
Introduction: Provide a clear introduction to the presentation. Make sure you cover the context, aim, and structure of the presentation. You may say something like this:

“We will be speaking on the article titled …, which was written by …, who specializes in the field of … as an investigative journalist. [i.e. the context] In this presentation, we will be providing you with the main highlights discussed in the article.., I will be speaking first to provide the introduction, and then X will be discussing the key messages, which will be followed by Y, who will conclude the takeaway message. [i.e. the structure]”
Conclusion: Make sure you conclude the presentation properly by covering: a summary, a key takeaway point/points, and closing remarks. This may sound like this:

“Overall, we found that the article provides an interesting insight into the industry, namely… [i.e. a takeaway point] … This concludes our presentation, and thank you very much for listening. Do you have any questions? [i.e. a closing remark]”

Stage 3 : Narratives
A good narrative makes the information relevant to the audience. It transforms the information into usable intelligence.
Story-telling is a good way of giving a good narrative.

Stage 4 : Delivery Style
Presentations as performance: Who presents, matters.

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
Delivery Tips — How You Present Matters
Amy Cuddy's TED Talk “Your Body Language May Shape Who You Are” — Key Insights:
Power postures affect confidence and how others perceive your competence
Eye contact, posture, voice projection, and pacing all communicate credibility
Practise out loud — reading silently and presenting aloud are very different skills

slides.title: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
text: FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 2
Visual Aids & Delivery — Best Practices
The 10-20-30 Rule (Guy Kawasaki) for presentations:
10 slides — the optimal number. More than 10 slides = losing your audience.
20 minutes — maximum speaking time to maintain audience attention and energy.
30 point font — minimum size. If you need to go smaller, you have too much text on that slide.

Situation → Complication → Question → Answer (SCQA) — the backbone of structured communication
